## Worked Problem 11.1: Disjoint Interval Packing vs. Minimum Interval Cover

### Problem & Constraints

You are given $N$ intervals $[L_i, R_i]$ ($L_i < R_i$) and a target range $[A, B]$. Solve two dual tasks on the same dataset:
1. **Task A (Disjoint Packing)**: Find the **maximum number of mutually disjoint** intervals you can select (two intervals $[L_i, R_i]$ and $[L_j, R_j]$ are disjoint if they share at most an endpoint, i.e., $R_i \le L_j$ or $R_j \le L_i$).
2. **Task B (Interval Covering)**: Find the **minimum number of intervals** whose union completely covers $[A, B]$, or report `-1` if impossible.

- $1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$
- $0 \le L_i < R_i \le 10^9$, $0 \le A < B \le 10^9$

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>In Task A (Disjoint Packing), why does sorting by left endpoint $L_i$ ascending fail, and why does sorting by shortest length $(R_i - L_i)$ ascending also fail?</li>
  <li>In Task B (Interval Covering), why must we switch to sorting by left endpoint $L_i$ ascending?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Both tasks can be modeled as shortest/longest path problems on a DAG of intervals after sorting, requiring $O(N^2)$ transitions if we test all predecessors $j < i$. To reduce $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$, we must identify the **single dominating transition** at each step.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

1. **Tempting Mistake 1 (Sorting by $L_i$ ascending for Disjoint Packing)**:
   - **Counterexample**: $[1, 10], [2, 4], [5, 8]$. The earliest-starting interval $[1, 10]$ spans the entire timeline and blocks both $[2, 4]$ and $[5, 8]$ ($1$ interval instead of $2$).
2. **Tempting Mistake 2 (Sorting by length $R_i - L_i$ ascending for Disjoint Packing)**:
   - **Counterexample**: $[1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10]$. The shortest interval is $[4, 7]$ (length $3$), which overlaps both $[1, 5]$ and $[6, 10]$ (lengths $4$ each), yielding $1$ interval instead of $2$!
3. **Tempting Mistake 3 (Sorting by $R_i$ descending for Covering)**:
   - Taking the interval with the largest $R_i$ globally may leave a gap on the left of $[A, B]$ that still requires extra intervals.

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Two Dual Structures

- **For Task A (Packing)**: Consider the very first interval in any valid disjoint set. All subsequent intervals must start at or after its right endpoint $R_1$. Therefore, choosing the interval with the **minimum possible right endpoint $R_{\min}$** maximizes the remaining timeline $[R_{\min}, \infty)$ available to all future choices!
- **For Task B (Covering $[A, B]$)**: Suppose we have already covered $[A, \text{cur}]$ completely. The next interval we pick **must** satisfy $L_i \le \text{cur}$ (otherwise a gap $(\text{cur}, L_i)$ remains uncovered). Among all intervals satisfying $L_i \le \text{cur}$, which one leaves the smallest remaining suffix $[\text{new\_cur}, B]$? The one with the **maximum right endpoint $R_i$**!

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Dual Endpoint Laws:</strong>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Disjoint Packing</strong>: Sort by $R_i$ ascending. Maintain $\text{last\_R} = -\infty$; whenever $L_i \ge \text{last\_R}$, take interval $i$ and set $\text{last\_R} = R_i$.</li>
  <li><strong>Minimum Covering</strong>: Sort by $L_i$ ascending. Maintain covered frontier $\text{cur} = A$. In each step, advance pointer $i$ through all intervals with $L_i \le \text{cur}$, tracking $\text{best\_R} = \max R_i$. If $\text{best\_R} \le \text{cur}$, coverage is impossible; otherwise set $\text{cur} = \text{best\_R}$ and increment count until $\text{cur} \ge B$.</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Implementation

**Stays-Ahead Proofs**:
- **Task A**: If greedy picks $g_1, \dots, g_k$ and any disjoint set picks $o_1, \dots, o_m$, then $R(g_1) \le R(o_1)$ by definition of minimum $R$. Assuming $R(g_{j-1}) \le R(o_{j-1})$, we have $L(o_j) \ge R(o_{j-1}) \ge R(g_{j-1})$, so $o_j$ is a valid candidate for $g_j$, meaning $R(g_j) \le R(o_j)$. Thus greedy never runs out of room before $O$, proving $k \ge m$.
- **Task B**: By induction on step $j$, the frontier $\text{cur}_j$ reached after $j$ greedy intervals is at least the frontier reached by the first $j$ intervals of any valid cover sorted by left endpoint.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

struct Interval {
    long long l, r;
};

int max_disjoint_packing(vector<Interval> a) {
    sort(a.begin(), a.end(), [](const Interval& x, const Interval& y) {
        if (x.r != y.r) return x.r < y.r;
        return x.l < y.l;
    });
    int count = 0;
    long long last_r = -4e18;
    for (const auto& iv : a) {
        if (iv.l >= last_r) {
            count++;
            last_r = iv.r;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int min_interval_cover(vector<Interval> a, long long A, long long B) {
    sort(a.begin(), a.end(), [](const Interval& x, const Interval& y) {
        if (x.l != y.l) return x.l < y.l;
        return x.r > y.r;
    });
    long long cur = A;
    int i = 0, n = static_cast<int>(a.size()), used = 0;
    while (cur < B) {
        long long best_r = cur;
        while (i < n && a[i].l <= cur) {
            best_r = max(best_r, a[i].r);
            i++;
        }
        if (best_r == cur) return -1; // Gap cannot be bridged
        cur = best_r;
        used++;
    }
    return used;
}
```

## Worked Problem 11.2: Weighted Radio Congestion (Event Sweep Line & Endpoint Tie-Breaking)

### Problem & Constraints

There are $N$ radio broadcasts. Broadcast $i$ transmits with power $w_i > 0$ over the time interval $[L_i, R_i)$. Find:
1. The **maximum total active power** at any real instant $t$, and the **earliest coordinate $t$** at which this maximum begins.
2. Explain clearly how the answer changes if the intervals are **closed** $[L_i, R_i]$ instead of half-open $[L_i, R_i)$.

- $1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$
- $0 \le L_i < R_i \le 10^{18}$, $1 \le w_i \le 10^9$

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>Suppose Broadcast 1 is on $[1, 5)$ with $w_1 = 10$ and Broadcast 2 is on $[5, 9)$ with $w_2 = 10$. What is the true maximum power on $[1, 9)$?</li>
  <li>What happens if you sort events at $t = 5$ with `+10` before `-10` and update the maximum right between them?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Let $P(t) = \sum_{i : t \in I_i} w_i$ be the total power at coordinate $t$. Since coordinates reach $10^{18}$, allocating a difference array of size $\max R_i$ is impossible. However, $P(t)$ is a **piecewise-constant step function** whose value can only change at the $2N$ coordinates $\{L_1, R_1, \dots, L_N, R_N\}$.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Tempting Mistake**: Create events `(L_i, +w_i)` and `(R_i, -w_i)`, sort them, and update `ans = max(ans, active)` after **every single event** without grouping equal coordinates (or using the wrong tie-breaker between `+w` and `-w`).

**Concrete 2-Broadcast Counterexample ($N = 2$)**:
- Broadcast 1: $[1, 5)$ with weight $w_1 = 10$.
- Broadcast 2: $[5, 9)$ with weight $w_2 = 10$.
- Under **half-open** semantics $[L_i, R_i)$, Broadcast 1 is already off at $t = 5$ when Broadcast 2 turns on. Thus $P(t) = 10$ for all $t \in [1, 9)$.
- If we process `(5, +10)` before `(5, -10)` and update `ans` in between, `active` momentarily hits $10 + 10 = 20$ at a phantom zero-length transition! Conversely, under **closed** semantics $[L_i, R_i]$, both broadcasts *are* simultaneously active at the exact point $t = 5$, so the maximum on closed intervals really is $20$!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure (Coordinate Grouping vs. Tie-Breaking)

There are two crystal-clear ways to handle equal event coordinates without ever making an off-by-one mistake:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Rule 1 — Half-Open Intervals $[L_i, R_i)$ (Coordinate Grouping):</strong>
Sort all events $(x, \Delta)$ by coordinate $x$ ascending. At each distinct coordinate $x_k$, <strong>sum all $\Delta$ values sharing $x_k$ first</strong>, and only then evaluate `active` as the true constant power on the non-empty Elementary Interval $[x_k, x_{k+1})$.
<br/><br/>
<strong>Rule 2 — Closed Intervals $[L_i, R_i]$ (Start-Before-End Tie-Breaking):</strong>
At a single point $x$, any interval starting at $x$ ($L_i = x$) and any interval ending at $x$ ($R_j = x$) overlap at point $x$ itself! To capture the peak at point $x$, either:
<ul>
  <li>Convert closed $[L_i, R_i]$ on integers to half-open $[L_i, R_i + 1)$ and use Rule 1, OR</li>
  <li>Sort events at equal $x$ with <strong>start events (`+w_i`) before end events (`-w_j`)</strong>.</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 4 — Progressive Construction & Visual Trace

Let us contrast Half-Open $[L_i, R_i)$ vs. Closed $[L_i, R_i]$ on $[1, 5, w=10], [3, 7, w=5], [5, 8, w=12]$:

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Implementation

**Elementary Interval Invariant**:
Let $x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_m$ be the sorted unique coordinates among all $L_i$ and $R_i$. Every half-open interval $[L_i, R_i)$ is the disjoint union of elementary intervals $[x_k, x_{k+1})$ for $L_i \le x_k < R_i$. After accumulating all $\Delta$ values at $x_1, \dots, x_k$, the prefix sum $\sum_{r=1}^k \Delta(x_r)$ adds $+w_i$ if $L_i \le x_k$ and $-w_i$ if $R_i \le x_k$, which contributes $w_i$ if and only if $L_i \le x_k < R_i$.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

struct Event {
    long long x;
    long long delta;
};

// Solves the half-open [L_i, R_i) maximum power and earliest time t
pair<long long, long long> solve_half_open_sweep(const vector<pair<long long, long long>>& intervals,
                                                 const vector<long long>& w) {
    vector<Event> ev;
    ev.reserve(intervals.size() * 2);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < intervals.size(); ++i) {
        ev.push_back({intervals[i].first, +w[i]});
        ev.push_back({intervals[i].second, -w[i]});
    }
    sort(ev.begin(), ev.end(), [](const Event& a, const Event& b) {
        return a.x < b.x;
    });

    long long active = 0, best_power = 0, best_time = 0;
    size_t i = 0;
    while (i < ev.size()) {
        long long coord = ev[i].x;
        while (i < ev.size() && ev[i].x == coord) {
            active += ev[i].delta;
            i++;
        }
        // Only evaluate if a non-empty span [coord, next_coord) follows
        if (i < ev.size() && active > best_power) {
            best_power = active;
            best_time = coord;
        }
    }
    return {best_power, best_time};
}
```

# Section 12 — Stacks, Queues, and Deques

## The Discovery & Modeling Approach

In an array $A[1 \dots N]$, why do naive nearest-smaller/larger scans and sliding-window extremum queries take $O(N^2)$? Because they repeatedly inspect elements that have already been **permanently dominated** by a newer, better element!

A **Monotonic Stack** or **Monotonic Deque** is nothing more than a standard container coupled with a **Dominance Pruning Rule**: whenever a new element $A[i]$ arrives, we immediately pop every older element that can never again win against $A[i]$ for any future query. Because each of the $N$ indices is pushed once and popped at most once, the amortized time per element drops from $O(N)$ to **$O(1)$**.

### Decision Compass: Monotonic Containers & Contribution Counting

| Structure | Problem Pattern | What the Container Stores | Dominance Pruning Rule (When $A[i]$ Arrives) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Monotonic Stack (Next/Prev Smaller)** | Find nearest element $< A[i]$ to the left and right | Indices with **strictly increasing** values from bottom to top | Pop indices $s$ while $A[s] \ge A[i]$ (newer element $i$ is both closer and smaller!) |
| **Contribution of Subarray Minima / Maxima** | Compute $\sum_{1 \le l \le r \le N} \min(A[l \dots r])$ | Span $[L_i, R_i]$ where $A[i]$ is the minimum | To avoid double-counting duplicates, use **strict `<` on one side** ($A[L_i] < A[i]$) and **non-strict `<=` on the other** ($A[R_i] \le A[i]$) |
| **Monotonic Deque (Sliding Window Min/Max)** | Maintain $\min / \max$ over moving window $[l, r]$ | Indices $j \in [l, r]$ with **monotonic values** from front to back | Back: pop $s$ while $A[s] \ge A[r]$ (for min); Front: pop $s$ while $s < l$ (expired!) |

## Worked Problem 12.1: Subarray Minimum Dominance Sum

### Problem & Constraints

Given an integer array $A[1 \dots N]$, compute the sum of the minimum elements of all $\frac{N(N+1)}{2}$ contiguous subarrays:
$$S = \sum_{1 \le l \le r \le N} \min_{l \le k \le r} A[k]$$

- $1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$
- $1 \le A[i] \le 10^9$ (Note: values may contain duplicates!)

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>Instead of iterating over all $\binom{N+1}{2}$ pairs $(l, r)$, how many subarrays $[l, r]$ have $A[i]$ as their minimum?</li>
  <li>If $A = [2, 2]$, both elements equal $2$. If both claim the full array $[1, 2]$ as their dominance span, what goes wrong?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Enumerating all pairs $(l, r)$ and maintaining the running minimum $\min(A[l \dots r])$ takes $O(N^2)$ time, which requires $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ operations for $N = 2 \cdot 10^5$. We must invert the summation from **"sum over subarrays of their minimum"** to **"sum over each index $i$ of $A[i] \times (\text{number of subarrays where } i \text{ is the canonical minimum})$"**.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

1. **Tempting Mistake 1 (Using `<` on both sides for $L_i$ and $R_i$)**:
   - Let $L_i$ be the nearest index $< i$ with $A[L_i] < A[i]$ and $R_i$ be the nearest index $> i$ with $A[R_i] < A[i]$.
   - **Counterexample**: $A = [2, 2]$.
     - For $i = 1$: $L_1 = 0, R_1 = 3 \implies (1 - 0)(3 - 1) = 2$ subarrays ($[1, 1]$ and $[1, 2]$).
     - For $i = 2$: $L_2 = 0, R_2 = 3 \implies (2 - 0)(3 - 2) = 2$ subarrays ($[2, 2]$ and $[1, 2]$).
     - Subarray $[1, 2]$ is **counted twice**, giving $2(2) + 2(2) = 8$ instead of $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$!
2. **Tempting Mistake 2 (Using `<=` on both sides)**:
   - On $A = [2, 2]$, $i = 1$ stops at $R_1 = 2$ and $i = 2$ stops at $L_2 = 1$, so subarray $[1, 2]$ is **counted zero times**!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Asymmetric Tie-Breaking Rule

To partition all subarrays cleanly without overlaps or omissions, define the **canonical minimum** of any subarray $[l, r]$ to be the **leftmost** index $i \in [l, r]$ that achieves $\min(A[l \dots r])$.

When is $i$ the leftmost minimum of $[l, r]$?
- Every element to the left of $i$ in $[l, i-1]$ must be **strictly greater** than $A[i]$: $A[k] > A[i]$ for $l \le k < i$.
- Every element to the right of $i$ in $[i+1, r]$ must be **greater than or equal** to $A[i]$: $A[k] \ge A[i]$ for $i < k \le r$.

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Asymmetric Dominance Boundaries:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>$L_i$: largest index $< i$ such that $A[L_i] \mathbf{<} A[i]$ (or $0$ if none).</li>
  <li>$R_i$: smallest index $> i$ such that $A[R_i] \mathbf{\le} A[i]$ (or $N+1$ if none).</li>
  <li>Number of subarrays with canonical minimum at $i$:
    $$\text{ways}(i) = (i - L_i) \times (R_i - i), \qquad S = \sum_{i=1}^N A[i] \cdot (i - L_i)(R_i - i)$$
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Implementation

**Bijection Proof**:
Every subarray $[l, r]$ has a non-empty set of indices achieving $\min_{l \le k \le r} A[k]$, and therefore a **unique minimum index** (the leftmost one, say $i^*$). By definition of leftmost minimum, no index in $[l, i^*-1]$ has value $\le A[i^*]$ (so $l > L_{i^*}$), and no index in $[i^*+1, r]$ has value $< A[i^*]$. Wait—note the symmetry in our table: in our table, $R_i$ stopped at $\le$ and $L_i$ stopped at $<$, which corresponds to $i^*$ being the **rightmost** minimum of $[l, r]$! Either convention (`<` left, `<=` right = rightmost minimum; `<=` left, `<` right = leftmost minimum) establishes a 1-to-1 bijection between all $\binom{N+1}{2}$ subarrays and the disjoint sets of pairs $(l, r) \in (L_i, i] \times [i, R_i)$.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

long long sum_of_subarray_minima(const vector<long long>& a) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(a.size());
    vector<int> L(n, -1), R(n, n);
    vector<int> st;

    // Single pass: when a[i] <= a[st.back()], i is the first index to the right with a[R] <= a[top]
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        while (!st.empty() && a[st.back()] >= a[i]) {
            R[st.back()] = i;
            st.pop_back();
        }
        L[i] = st.empty() ? -1 : st.back();
        st.push_back(i);
    }

    long long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long ways = 1LL * (i - L[i]) * (R[i] - i);
        total += a[i] * ways;
    }
    return total;
}
```

## Worked Problem 12.2: Bounded-Turbulence Flight Window (Dual Monotonic Deques)

### Problem & Constraints

Given $N$ sensor readings $A[1 \dots N]$ and a tolerance $K \ge 0$, find the length of the **longest contiguous subarray** $[l, r]$ such that the spread between its maximum and minimum reading satisfies:
$$\max_{l \le i \le r} A[i] - \min_{l \le i \le r} A[i] \le K$$

- $1 \le N \le 5 \cdot 10^5$
- $0 \le K \le 10^9$, $1 \le A[i] \le 10^9$

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>Why is the spread condition $\max(A[l \dots r]) - \min(A[l \dots r]) \le K$ **window-monotone** as $l$ and $r$ move rightward?</li>
  <li>Why would using a `std::multiset` cost $O(N \log N)$ with high constant factor, whereas two `std::deque`s achieve $O(N)$ with tiny constant factor?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Expanding $[l, r]$ adds elements, which can only **increase** $\max(A[l \dots r])$ and **decrease** $\min(A[l \dots r])$, so the spread $\text{spread}(l, r) = \max - \min$ is monotonically non-decreasing as the window grows. Thus for each right endpoint $r$, the earliest valid left endpoint $l^*(r)$ moves monotonically rightward!

However, when we advance $l \to l+1$ to shrink an invalid window, how do we know the new $\max$ and $\min$ of $[l+1, r]$ without rescanning the window in $O(N)$?

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Tempting Mistake**: Store only two scalar variables `cur_min` and `cur_max`, and try to reset them when $A[l]$ leaves the window.
- **Counterexample**: $A = [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]$, $K = 4$. When $[1, 4]$ has `cur_min = 1` at index $2$ and $l$ advances past index $2$, the new minimum of $[3, 4]$ is $2$ (at index $4$), not $4$ (at index $3$). Without maintaining the **ascending chain of suffix minima** inside the window, you must rescan!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Dual Monotonic Deque Architecture

Maintain two deques of indices inside $[l, r]$:
1. `min_dq`: indices with **strictly increasing** values from front to back (`A[min_dq.front()]` is $\min(A[l \dots r])$).
2. `max_dq`: indices with **strictly decreasing** values from front to back (`A[max_dq.front()]` is $\max(A[l \dots r])$).

When advancing $r$:
- Pop from `min_dq.back()` while $A[\text{back}] \ge A[r]$, then push $r$.
- Pop from `max_dq.back()` while $A[\text{back}] \le A[r]$, then push $r$.
- While $A[\text{max\_dq.front()}] - A[\text{min\_dq.front()}] > K$, increment $l$, and if either deque's `front()` equals $l - 1$, pop it from the front!

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Amortized $O(N)$ Window Spread Invariant:</strong>
At the end of iteration $r$, $l$ is the smallest index $\le r$ such that $A[\text{max\_dq.front()}] - A[\text{min\_dq.front()}] \le K$, and the longest valid window ending at $r$ has length $r - l + 1$.
</div>

### Step 4 — Progressive Construction & Visual Trace

Let us trace $A = [4, 2, 5, 7, 3]$ with $K = 3$:

  <!-- Step boxes -->

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Implementation

**Why Each Element Enters and Leaves Each Deque at Most Once**:
Index $r$ is pushed to the back of `min_dq` and `max_dq` once at iteration $r$. Any element popped from the back at iteration $r$ is both **older** ($j < r$) and **less extreme** than $A[r]$, so for every future window $[l, r']$ containing $r' \ge r$, index $r$ outlives $j$ and beats $j$'s value. Thus popped elements never re-enter, giving strict $O(N)$ time.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int longest_bounded_spread(const vector<long long>& a, long long K) {
    deque<int> min_dq, max_dq;
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < static_cast<int>(a.size()); ++r) {
        while (!min_dq.empty() && a[min_dq.back()] >= a[r]) min_dq.pop_back();
        min_dq.push_back(r);

        while (!max_dq.empty() && a[max_dq.back()] <= a[r]) max_dq.pop_back();
        max_dq.push_back(r);

        while (a[max_dq.front()] - a[min_dq.front()] > K) {
            if (min_dq.front() == l) min_dq.pop_front();
            if (max_dq.front() == l) max_dq.pop_front();
            l++;
        }
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
```

# Section 13 — Offline Processing

## The Discovery & Modeling Approach

A problem is **online** if each query must be answered before the next query is revealed (e.g., when the next query's parameters are encrypted with the previous answer). Whenever all $Q$ queries are given in the input up front and no such dependency exists, you are free to **reorder the queries** into whatever sequence makes maintaining the data structure easiest, compute their answers, and print them in their original order `ans[q.id]`.

That simple freedom—**Offline Processing**—regularly turns 2D data structure nightmares (which would otherwise require $O(N \log^2 N)$ Merge-Sort Trees or Persistent Segment Trees) into a single $O((N + Q) \log N)$ sweep with a humble Fenwick Tree or DSU!

### Decision Compass: How to Choose the Offline Sweep Dimension

| Sub-Pattern | 2D Query Condition | Offline Sweep Order | Maintained 1D Structure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Threshold Activation Sweep** | "In subarray $[L, R]$, count / sum elements with $A[i] \ge X$" (or edges with weight $\le W$) | Sort both array elements $A[i]$ and queries $(L, R, X)$ by **threshold $X$ descending** | Fenwick Tree (or DSU for graphs) where index $i$ is activated (`add(i, 1)`) once $A[i] \ge X$ |
| **Right-Endpoint Sweep with Last Occurrence** | "In subarray $[L, R]$, count **distinct** values" (or minimum duplicate distance) | Sort queries by **right endpoint $R$ ascending**; sweep $r = 1 \dots N$ | Fenwick Tree with $+1$ at **only the latest occurrence** `last[v]` of each value $v \in A[1 \dots r]$ |
| **Divide-and-Conquer / Mo's Ordering** | Non-decomposable range queries without updates | Sort queries by $(\lfloor L / B \rfloor, R)$ with $B \approx N / \sqrt{Q}$ | Incremental `add(idx)` / `remove(idx)` state in $O((N+Q)\sqrt{N})$ |

## Worked Problem 13.1: Historical Rank Queries (Threshold-Sorted Offline Activation)

### Problem & Constraints

You are given an array $A[1 \dots N]$ of $N$ scores and $Q$ queries. Query $q$ gives $(L_q, R_q, X_q)$ and asks: **How many elements in the subarray $A[L_q \dots R_q]$ satisfy $A[i] \ge X_q$?**

- $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$
- $1 \le A[i], X_q \le 10^9$

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>Why can't a standard static prefix sum array answer $(L_q, R_q, X_q)$ for arbitrary $X_q$?</li>
  <li>If you sort the queries in descending order of $X_q$, what happens to the set of indices $\{i : A[i] \ge X_q\}$ as you move from one query to the next?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Each query asks for the number of points $(i, A[i])$ inside the 2D rectangle $[L_q, R_q] \times [X_q, \infty)$. Scanning $[L_q, R_q]$ per query takes $O(Q N)$ time. Building a Merge-Sort Tree over $A[1 \dots N]$ and binary searching in $O(\log N)$ nodes per query takes $O(Q \log^2 N)$ time and $O(N \log N)$ memory. Can we strip away a $\log N$ factor and use a simple $O(N)$-word Fenwick Tree?

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

1. **Tempting Mistake 1 (Sorting queries by $L_q$ or $R_q$ instead of $X_q$)**:
   - If you sweep $R_q$ from $1$ to $N$ while $X_q$ jumps arbitrarily up and down, you still need a dynamic rank tree over values (which requires coordinate compression). Sorting by $X_q$ makes the value threshold monotone and requires zero coordinate compression!
2. **Tempting Mistake 2 (Forgetting original query IDs or tie-breaking elements vs. queries)**:
   - **Counterexample**: Suppose $A = [5, 5]$ and a query asks for $X_q = 5$ on $[1, 2]$. If you process the query at threshold $5$ *before* activating array elements with $A[i] = 5$, you report $0$ instead of $2$!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Monotone Activation Invariant

As the threshold $X_q$ decreases from $\infty$ down to $-\infty$, the condition $A[i] \ge X_q$ transitions **once** for each index $i$ from `false` to `true` and never turns back to `false`!

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Offline Threshold Sweep Blueprint:</strong>
<ol>
  <li>Pair each array element as $(A[i], i)$ and sort in <strong>descending order of value $A[i]$</strong>.</li>
  <li>Store each query as $(X_q, L_q, R_q, \text{id})$ and sort in <strong>descending order of threshold $X_q$</strong>.</li>
  <li>Maintain a 1D Fenwick Tree `bit` of size $N$ (initially all $0$) and a pointer `ptr` into the sorted array elements.</li>
  <li>For each query $q$: while `ptr < N` and `elem[ptr].val >= q.X`, call `bit.add(elem[ptr].idx, +1)` and advance `ptr`. Then `ans[q.id] = bit.query(q.L, q.R)`.</li>
</ol>
</div>

Let $A = [4, 9, 2, 7, 6]$ and consider queries $Q_1 = (L=1, R=4, X=5)$ and $Q_2 = (L=2, R=5, X=7)$.

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Implementation

**Proof of Invariant**:
Because `elems` and `queries` are both sorted in non-increasing order of value/threshold, when query $q$ is evaluated, the `while` loop has inserted every element with $A[i] \ge X_q$ and no element with $A[i] < X_q$. Thus `bit[i] = 1` if and only if $A[i] \ge X_q$, so $\sum_{i=L_q}^{R_q} \text{bit}[i]$ is the exact count. Each of the $N$ elements is inserted into the Fenwick tree at most once, yielding $O((N + Q) \log N)$ total time.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<int> tree;
    explicit Fenwick(int n) : n(n), tree(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, int delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) tree[i] += delta;
    }
    int query(int i) const {
        int s = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += tree[i];
        return s;
    }
    int query(int l, int r) const { return query(r) - query(l - 1); }
};

struct Query {
    int l, r;
    long long x;
    int id;
};

vector<int> solve_historical_rank(const vector<long long>& a, vector<Query> queries) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(a.size());
    vector<pair<long long, int>> elems(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) elems[i] = {a[i], i + 1};

    sort(elems.begin(), elems.end(), greater<pair<long long, int>>());
    sort(queries.begin(), queries.end(), [](const Query& u, const Query& v) {
        return u.x > v.x;
    });

    Fenwick bit(n);
    vector<int> ans(queries.size());
    int ptr = 0;
    for (const auto& q : queries) {
        while (ptr < n && elems[ptr].first >= q.x) {
            bit.add(elems[ptr].second, 1);
            ptr++;
        }
        ans[q.id] = bit.query(q.l, q.r);
    }
    return ans;
}
```

## Worked Problem 13.2: Distinct Frequency Range Audit (Right-Endpoint Sweep & Last-Occurrence Shift)

### Problem & Constraints

Given an array $A[1 \dots N]$ and $Q$ range queries $[L_q, R_q]$, report for each query the **number of distinct values** that appear at least once in $A[L_q \dots R_q]$.

- $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$
- $1 \le A[i] \le 10^9$

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong>
<ul>
  <li>Why can't you compute `distinct(1, R) - distinct(1, L - 1)` to get the number of distinct elements in $[L, R]$?</li>
  <li>Suppose you fix the right endpoint $R$ and want to answer $[L, R]$ for any $L \le R$. If value $v$ appears at indices $2, 5$, and $8$ inside $1 \dots R$, which single index of $v$ determines whether $v$ appears in $[L, R]$?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

A value $v$ appears in $[L, R]$ if and only if $\{i \in [L, R] : A[i] = v\} \ne \emptyset$. Because multiple copies of $v$ inside $[L, R]$ contribute only **once** to the distinct count, a static prefix sum counts total elements, not distinct elements. Computing `std::unordered_set` per query takes $O(Q N)$ time.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Tempting Mistake**: Try to use `prefix_distinct[R] - prefix_distinct[L - 1]`.
- **Counterexample**: $A = [7, 3, 7]$.
  - `prefix_distinct` is $[1, 2, 2]$.
  - For query $[L=2, R=3]$ (subarray $[3, 7]$), there are $2$ distinct values, yet `prefix_distinct[3] - prefix_distinct[1] = 2 - 1 = 1` because value $7$ appeared both before $L$ (at index $1$) and inside $[L, R]$ (at index $3$)!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Last-Occurrence Canonical Representative

Why did `prefix_distinct` fail on $A = [7, 3, 7]$ for query $[2, 3]$? Because we placed the $+1$ credit for value $7$ at its **first** occurrence (index $1$), which fell to the left of $L = 2$ even though a later copy of $7$ existed at index $3 \in [2, 3]$!

Now flip that convention when fixing the right endpoint $r$:
> Among all occurrences of value $v$ in the prefix $A[1 \dots r]$, let $\text{last}_r(v)$ be the **rightmost (latest)** index $\le r$ where $A[i] = v$. Then:
> $$v \text{ appears in } A[L \dots r] \iff \text{last}_r(v) \ge L$$

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Right-Endpoint Last-Occurrence Invariant:</strong>
Group all queries $[L_q, R_q]$ by their right endpoint $R_q$. Sweep $r$ from $1$ to $N$:
<ol>
  <li>If $v = A[r]$ appeared previously at $\text{last}[v] > 0$, remove its old marker: <code>bit.add(last[v], -1)</code>.</li>
  <li>Place the marker at the new latest position: <code>last[v] = r; bit.add(r, +1)</code>.</li>
  <li>For every query $(L_q, r)$ ending at $r$, the number of distinct values in $[L_q, r]$ is <code>bit.query(L_q, r)</code>!</li>
</ol>
</div>

### Step 4 — Progressive Construction & Visual Trace

Let us trace $A = [7, 3, 7, 5]$ as $r$ sweeps from $1$ to $4$:

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Bijection Between Distinct Values in $[L, r]$ and Active Markers in $[L, r]$**:
At the end of step $r$:
1. Every distinct value $v$ present in $A[1 \dots r]$ has **exactly one** $+1$ marker in the Fenwick tree, located at $i = \text{last}_r(v) \le r$.
2. If $v$ occurs at least once in $A[L \dots r]$, then its rightmost occurrence in $A[1 \dots r]$ certainly satisfies $L \le \text{last}_r(v) \le r$, so its unique marker lies inside $[L, r]$ and contributes $+1$ to `bit.query(L, r)`.
3. Conversely, if $v$ does not occur in $A[L \dots r]$, then either $v$ never appeared in $A[1 \dots r]$ or all of its occurrences in $A[1 \dots r]$ lie strictly to the left of $L$ ($\text{last}_r(v) < L$), so its marker contributes $0$ to `bit.query(L, r)`.

*(Implementation Tip: Coordinate-compress $A[1 \dots N]$ into $0 \dots U-1$ first so `last[v]` is a flat `vector<int>` instead of a slower hash table!)*

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<int> tree;
    explicit Fenwick(int n) : n(n), tree(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, int delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) tree[i] += delta;
    }
    int query(int i) const {
        int s = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += tree[i];
        return s;
    }
    int query(int l, int r) const { return query(r) - query(l - 1); }
};

struct RangeQuery {
    int l, r, id;
};

vector<int> solve_distinct_offline(const vector<long long>& a, const vector<RangeQuery>& queries) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(a.size());
    // Coordinate compression for O(1) array lookup of last occurrence
    vector<long long> vals = a;
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());

    vector<int> comp(n + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
        comp[i] = static_cast<int>(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), a[i - 1]) - vals.begin());
    }

    vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> by_r(n + 1);
    for (const auto& q : queries) {
        by_r[q.r].push_back({q.l, q.id});
    }

    Fenwick bit(n);
    vector<int> last(vals.size(), 0);
    vector<int> ans(queries.size());

    for (int r = 1; r <= n; ++r) {
        int v = comp[r];
        if (last[v] != 0) {
            bit.add(last[v], -1);
        }
        last[v] = r;
        bit.add(r, +1);

        for (const auto& [l, id] : by_r[r]) {
            ans[id] = bit.query(l, r);
        }
    }
    return ans;
}
```

# Section 15 — BFS and Unweighted Shortest Paths

## The Discovery & Modeling Approach

In competitive programming, very few Breadth-First Search (BFS) problems begin with the sentence *"Given an unweighted graph $G = (V, E)$, find the shortest path from $s$ to $t$."* Instead, the problem describes a discrete system—a grid of rooms, a mechanical lock, a set of jugs, a token moving along an array, or a spreading flood—and asks for the **minimum number of elementary steps, turns, or operations** required to reach a target configuration.

The fundamental discovery task in Section 15 is recognizing that **"minimum number of unit-cost actions"** is synonymous with **"shortest path in an unweighted state graph."** Whenever every legal action advances a clock by $+1$ (or costs $1$ unit of an identical resource) and the feasibility of future actions depends only on a bounded snapshot of the current configuration, BFS is the canonical solver.

### Recognizing Hidden Unweighted Shortest Path Problems

Look for the following structural cues in a problem statement and its constraints:

1. **Uniform Step Cost:** Every valid transition increments the answer by $+1$. There are no variable edge weights, discounts, or free moves (which would point to 0-1 BFS in Section 20 or Dijkstra in Section 19).
2. **Small Total State Volume:** If the graph is not given explicitly, multiply the sizes of the parameters needed to describe a configuration. If $\prod |D_i| \le 2 \cdot 10^6$ and the branching factor (out-degree per state) is a small constant, the implicit state graph fits comfortably in an $O(V + E)$ traversal.
3. **Simultaneous Spreading Processes:** If multiple origins expand at the same rate (e.g., fire, water, monsters, or signal towers) and you need either the earliest arrival time at every cell or a safe path that strictly beats the hazard at every step, the wave property of BFS allows all sources to be merged into a single pass.
4. **First-Visit Optimality:** Because a FIFO queue processes vertices in nondecreasing order of distance $d = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, the **very first time** a state is generated, its distance is guaranteed to be optimal.

### Decision Compass & Structural Lenses

| Sub-Pattern | Signal in the Problem Statement | Graph / Queue Construction | Complexity & Invariant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard Point-to-Point BFS** | "Minimum moves/hops from $s$ to $t$" on an explicit network or grid. | Push $s$ with $\text{dist}[s]=0$; relax unvisited neighbors to $\text{dist}[u]+1$. | $O(V + E)$ time. Queue holds at most two consecutive distance layers $d$ and $d+1$. |
| **Multi-Source Wavefront BFS** | "Nearest special node to every vertex" or "hazard spreads from all $k$ origins simultaneously." | Push **all** sources $s_1, \dots, s_k$ into the queue at $\text{dist} = 0$ before popping anything. | $O(V + E)$ total (replaces $k$ separate runs). Equivalent to adding a virtual super-source $S^*$. |
| **Two-Pass Hazard-Evasion BFS** | "Reach the exit before a spreading hazard reaches any cell you step on." | Pass 1: Multi-source BFS from all hazards to get $H[v]$. Pass 2: Player BFS allowing $u \to v$ iff $\text{dist}[u]+1 < H[v]$. | $O(V + E)$ in two decoupled phases whenever the hazard's spread is independent of the player. |
| **Implicit State-Space BFS** | Rules depend on auxiliary context: orientation, remainder $\bmod K$, last move, or a bitmask of $b \le 10$ switches. | Define vertex as tuple $\mathbf{x} = (u, r, \text{mask})$. Allocate $\text{dist}[u][r][\text{mask}]$. | $O(V_{\text{state}} + E_{\text{state}})$. Safely compresses path history into a Markovian tuple. |
| **Shortest Cycle / Girth via BFS** | "Find the shortest cycle in an undirected unweighted graph" ($N \le 2000$). | Run BFS from each vertex $r$; when inspecting edge $(u, v)$ where $v \neq \text{parent}[u]$ is already visited, candidate cycle is $\text{dist}[u] + \text{dist}[v] + 1$. | $O(V(V + E))$. The first non-tree edge encountered is within $+1$ of the minimum cycle through $r$. |

## Worked Problem 15.1: Cryogenic Spill Containment

### Problem & Constraints

A research facility is modeled as an $R \times C$ grid of rooms ($1 \le R, C \le 1000$). Each cell is one of:
- `.` : an open corridor,
- `#` : a sealed bulkhead (impassable to both personnel and coolant),
- `L` : a ruptured cryogenic tank (there may be between $1$ and $R \cdot C$ ruptured tanks),
- `S` : the technician's starting position (exactly one),
- `E` : the emergency extraction airlock (exactly one).

At time $t = 0$, cryogenic vapor occupies all `L` cells. At each integer second $t = 1, 2, \dots$, the vapor simultaneously expands from every currently contaminated cell into all four-directionally adjacent non-bulkhead cells (`.`, `S`, and `E`). Simultaneously, during each second, the technician may move from their current cell to any four-directionally adjacent non-bulkhead cell. The technician **cannot** step into a cell at time $t$ if the vapor reaches that cell at or before time $t$ (including the extraction airlock `E`).

Find the minimum number of seconds required for the technician to reach `E`, or report `-1` if no safe route exists.

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong> Before reading further, ask yourself:
<ul>
  <li>If there are $5 \cdot 10^5$ ruptured tanks, why does running a separate BFS from each tank time out?</li>
  <li>Does the technician's movement alter how the cryogenic vapor spreads? What does that independence allow us to precompute?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

In a brute-force simulation, the system state at time $t$ consists of the technician's position $(r, c)$ together with the exact subset of cells currently flooded by vapor. Alternatively, to check if the technician can step onto cell $(r, c)$ at time $t$, we need to know whether **any** ruptured tank $L_i$ is at Manhattan-walk distance $\le t$ from $(r, c)$ around the bulkheads.

If there are $K$ ruptured tanks and we run an independent BFS from each tank $L_i$ to compute its arrival time at every cell, the work is:
$$\Theta(K \cdot R \cdot C)$$
When $R = C = 1000$, $R \cdot C = 10^6$, and $K$ can be on the order of $10^6$. That yields $10^{12}$ operations—four orders of magnitude beyond the 1-second budget.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Mistake 1: Using Manhattan distance to the nearest `L` instead of graph distance.**\
Bulkheads (`#`) block the vapor just as they block the technician. A tank at $(1, 1)$ separated from $(1, 3)$ by a wall at $(1, 2)$ takes more than $2$ seconds to reach $(1, 3)$.

**Mistake 2: Interleaving a single queue where the technician pushes before/after vapor without precomputing hazard times, or letting vapor overwrite `E` in place without checking exact arrival parity.**\
Suppose you run a single queue and push `S` first, then all `L` cells, marking cells as blocked when visited. If `S` expands into cell $X$ at $t=1$, and `L` also expands into $X$ at $t=1$, pushing `S` first lets the technician illegally claim $X$ before the vapor's $t=1$ transition is processed!

**Concrete Small Counterexample:**
```text
L . S
# . #
# E #
```
Here `S` is at $(1, 3)$ and `L` is at $(1, 1)$. Both are adjacent to $(1, 2)$. At $t = 1$, both `L` and `S` reach $(1, 2)$. Since the technician cannot enter a cell at the exact moment vapor arrives ($t_{\text{tech}} = 1 \not< t_{\text{vapor}} = 1$), cell $(1, 2)$ is fatal. A naive interleaved queue that pops `S` before `L` at layer $t=0$ would mark $(1, 2)$ as safely visited by the technician at $t=1$ and falsely report distance $3$ to `E`.

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure

Notice two decoupling facts:
1. **The vapor spread is completely oblivious to the technician.** Whether the technician moves north, south, or stands still, the earliest time $H[r][c]$ at which vapor contaminates cell $(r, c)$ is fixed solely by the initial grid.
2. **All ruptured tanks are indistinguishable.** Cell $(r, c)$ is contaminated at time:
   $$H[r][c] = \min_{i=1}^{K} \text{dist}_{\text{grid}}(L_i, (r, c))$$

Instead of $K$ separate BFS runs, imagine introducing a conceptual **super-source** $S^*$ connected by zero-length edges to every ruptured tank $L_i$. In practice, we don't even need to create $S^*$: we simply initialize a single FIFO queue with **all** $L_i$ cells at distance $0$. By the BFS layer invariant, the wave expands across all tanks simultaneously in $O(RC)$ total time, filling the exact table $H[r][c]$.

Once $H[r][c]$ is static and known for every cell, the technician's problem reduces to a standard single-source BFS from `S` where a transition $(r, c) \to (nr, nc)$ at time $d + 1 = \text{dist}[r][c] + 1$ is legal if and only if:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Hazard-Evasion Feasibility Condition:</strong>
$$\text{ cell } (nr, nc) \neq \text{'\#'} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{dist}[r][c] + 1 < H[nr][nc]$$
</div>

- Row 0: `L . . S`
- Row 1: `# . # .`
- Row 2: `. . E .`

Notice how cell $(0, 2)$ is reachable at $d = 1 < H[0][2] = 2$, which turns out to be a dead end because $(0, 1)$ has $H[0][1] = 1 \le 2$. Meanwhile, moving south along column $3$ reaches `E` at $d = 3$, strictly beating $H[2][2] = 4$.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <queue>

using namespace std;

const int INF = 1e9;
const int dr[4] = {-1, 1, 0, 0};
const int dc[4] = {0, 0, -1, 1};

int solve() {
    int R, C;
    if (!(cin >> R >> C)) return 0;
    vector<string> grid(R);
    for (int r = 0; r < R; ++r) cin >> grid[r];

    vector<vector<int>> H(R, vector<int>(C, INF));
    queue<pair<int, int>> q_hazard;
    pair<int, int> start_pos, exit_pos;

    for (int r = 0; r < R; ++r) {
        for (int c = 0; c < C; ++c) {
            if (grid[r][c] == 'L') {
                H[r][c] = 0;
                q_hazard.push({r, c});
            } else if (grid[r][c] == 'S') {
                start_pos = {r, c};
            } else if (grid[r][c] == 'E') {
                exit_pos = {r, c};
            }
        }
    }

    // Pass 1: Multi-source BFS for cryogenic vapor arrival times
    while (!q_hazard.empty()) {
        auto [r, c] = q_hazard.front();
        q_hazard.pop();
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
            int nr = r + dr[i], nc = c + dc[i];
            if (nr >= 0 && nr < R && nc >= 0 && nc < C && grid[nr][nc] != '#') {
                if (H[nr][nc] > H[r][c] + 1) {
                    H[nr][nc] = H[r][c] + 1;
                    q_hazard.push({nr, nc});
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // Pass 2: Single-source BFS for the technician
    vector<vector<int>> dist(R, vector<int>(C, INF));
    queue<pair<int, int>> q_tech;

    dist[start_pos.first][start_pos.second] = 0;
    q_tech.push(start_pos);

    while (!q_tech.empty()) {
        auto [r, c] = q_tech.front();
        q_tech.pop();
        if (make_pair(r, c) == exit_pos) return dist[r][c];

        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
            int nr = r + dr[i], nc = c + dc[i];
            if (nr >= 0 && nr < R && nc >= 0 && nc < C && grid[nr][nc] != '#') {
                int next_time = dist[r][c] + 1;
                if (next_time < H[nr][nc] && dist[nr][nc] == INF) {
                    dist[nr][nc] = next_time;
                    q_tech.push({nr, nc});
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
```

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Proof of Soundness and Completeness:**
1. *Why waiting in place never helps:* Suppose a valid walk pauses at some cell $(r, c)$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ and then follows path $P$ to `E`. If the technician instead traverses $P$ one second earlier, every cell $(r', c') \in P$ is visited at time $t' - 1 < t' < H[r'][c']$. Because the upper bound $H[r'][c']$ depends only on cell coordinates and not on time, arriving earlier at $(r', c')$ strictly relaxes the inequality $t_{\text{visit}} < H[r'][c']$.
2. *Why first visit in Pass 2 is sufficient:* By (1), if any valid arrival time at $(r, c)$ can be extended to `E`, then the **earliest** arrival time $\text{dist}[r][c]$ can also be extended to `E`. Standard BFS discovers the minimum feasible arrival time at each cell upon first push.

**Small-Case Oracle:** For $R, C \le 4$, write a recursive backtracking oracle that steps time $t = 0, 1, \dots, R \cdot C$, explicitly expands the set of flooded cells at step $t$, and tries all 4 moves for the technician. Verify that the two-pass BFS matches on grids where `L` is disconnected by `#` walls (so $H = \infty$) and where `L` and `S` race for `E` at identical distances.

## Worked Problem 15.2: Resonance-Locked Courier

### Problem & Constraints

A pneumatic transit network has $N$ stations ($2 \le N \le 10^5$) and $M$ directed tubes ($1 \le M \le 2 \cdot 10^5$). Traversing any tube takes $1$ minute. However, the airlock at destination station $N$ is governed by a $K$-phase resonance cycle ($1 \le K \le 10$): it only opens at minutes $t$ that are exact multiples of $K$ ($t \equiv 0 \pmod K$). Furthermore, every station $u$ has a safety valve that forces a parcel to leave immediately upon arrival—waiting at a station is impossible.

Find the minimum time $t$ (which may be a multiple of $K$ greater than the geometric shortest path) to travel from station $1$ to station $N$ and exit through the open airlock, or report `-1` if no such walk exists.

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong> Before reading further, ask yourself:
<ul>
  <li>Why can't we just find the shortest path from $1$ to $N$ and check if its length is divisible by $K$?</li>
  <li>If two different walks arrive at station $u$ at times $t_1 = 3$ and $t_2 = 3 + 2K$, can one reach the open airlock at $N$ if and only if the other can?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

A walk is a sequence of directed edges $(u_0, u_1, \dots, u_t)$ with $u_0 = 1$, $u_t = N$, and $t \equiv 0 \pmod K$. Unlike standard shortest paths, the optimal walk **may not be a simple path**: it might need to traverse a directed cycle to adjust its length modulo $K$ before arriving at $N$.

Enumerating all walks of length up to $N \cdot K$ explores up to $\Delta^{NK}$ paths, which is exponential. Storing all reachable exact arrival times at every vertex $u$ is also unbounded if the graph has cycles.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Mistake: Running standard BFS to record only the single earliest arrival time $\text{dist}[u]$ at each vertex.**\
If standard BFS reaches $N$ at time $d \not\equiv 0 \pmod K$, it discards all slightly longer walks that arrive at intermediate vertices one or two steps later.

**Concrete Small Counterexample:**\
Let $N = 3, K = 3$, with edges:
- $1 \to 2 \to 3$ (length $2 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$), and
- an alternate detour $1 \to 4 \to 2$ (making path $1 \to 4 \to 2 \to 3$ of length $3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$).

Standard BFS visits vertex $2$ at $t = 1$ via $1 \to 2$ and marks vertex $2$ as visited. When the detour $1 \to 4 \to 2$ arrives at vertex $2$ at $t = 2$, standard BFS ignores it because $2 > 1$. Consequently, vertex $3$ is only ever reached at $t = 2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$, and the algorithm falsely outputs `-1`!

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure

Ask the compression question from the manual's introduction: *What information about the past walk actually affects whether a future continuation $(u \leadsto N)$ of length $L$ will satisfy $(t_{\text{so far}} + L) \equiv 0 \pmod K$?*

Only the remainder $r = t_{\text{so far}} \bmod K$ matters! If two walks arrive at station $u$ with the **same** remainder $r \in \{0, 1, \dots, K-1\}$, and one has total time $t_1$ while the other has $t_2 > t_1$, any valid suffix walk from $u$ to $N$ of length $L \equiv -r \pmod K$ works for both, and the first walk finishes strictly earlier ($t_1 + L < t_2 + L$).

Therefore, we lift each original station $u$ into $K$ state vertices:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Product State-Space Definition:</strong>
$$V_{\text{state}} = \{ (u, r) \mid u \in \{1, \dots, N\},\; r \in \{0, \dots, K-1\} \}$$
$$\text{Directed Transition: } (u, r) \longrightarrow \bigl(v, (r + 1) \bmod K\bigr) \quad \text{for every edge } u \to v \in E$$
</div>

In this lifted graph, there are $N \cdot K \le 10^6$ vertices and $M \cdot K \le 2 \cdot 10^6$ unit-cost edges. The target is the single state $(N, 0)$, starting from $(1, 0)$.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>

using namespace std;

const int INF = 1e9;

int solve() {
    int N, M, K;
    if (!(cin >> N >> M >> K)) return 0;
    vector<vector<int>> adj(N + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        cin >> u >> v;
        adj[u].push_back(v);
    }

    vector<vector<int>> dist(N + 1, vector<int>(K, INF));
    queue<pair<int, int>> q;

    dist[1][0] = 0;
    q.push({1, 0});

    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto [u, r] = q.front();
        q.pop();

        int nr = (r + 1) % K;
        for (int v : adj[u]) {
            if (dist[v][nr] == INF) {
                dist[v][nr] = dist[u][r] + 1;
                q.push({v, nr});
            }
        }
    }

    return (dist[N][0] == INF) ? -1 : dist[N][0];
}
```

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Two-Way Bijection Between Valid Walks and State Paths:**
- *Forward:* Every walk $1 = u_0 \to u_1 \to \dots \to u_L = N$ in $G$ lifts uniquely to the sequence of states $(u_0, 0) \to (u_1, 1 \bmod K) \to \dots \to (u_L, L \bmod K)$ in $G_{\text{state}}$. The walk satisfies $L \equiv 0 \pmod K$ if and only if its final state is $(N, 0)$.
- *Reverse:* Any shortest path in $G_{\text{state}}$ from $(1, 0)$ to $(N, 0)$ projects down to a valid walk in $G$ of the exact same edge count. Since $G_{\text{state}}$ has $N \cdot K$ vertices, any simple path in $G_{\text{state}}$ has length $< N \cdot K$, proving that an optimal walk never needs to exceed $N \cdot K$ steps.

# Section 16 — DFS, Components, and Cycles

## The Discovery & Modeling Approach

Whereas BFS explores a graph in concentric distance rings, Depth-First Search (DFS) plunges as deeply as possible along a path before backtracking. Why would we ever prefer DFS over BFS? Because **DFS imposes a rooted tree structure on any graph** and brackets every vertex's active lifetime into a contiguous time interval $[\text{tin}[u], \text{tout}[u]]$. Whenever a problem asks about **connectivity, cycle existence, structural decomposition, two-coloring (parity), or ancestral relationships**, the DFS tree turns messy global graph topology into clean local edge classifications.

### Recognizing Hidden DFS, Bipartite, and Functional Graph Problems

1. **Binary Equality / Inequality Constraints:** If a problem gives pairs of variables with "same team / opposite team", "equal / different parity", or "flip switch $A$ and $B$ to reach a target state", model variables as vertices and constraints as edges labeled $0$ (same) or $1$ (opposite). Feasibility reduces to checking whether any cycle has an odd sum of edge labels (generalized 2-coloring via DFS).
2. **Deadlocks and Circular Dependencies:** If directed transitions represent "process $A$ waits on process $B$", a deadlock exists iff DFS encounters an edge pointing to an **currently active ancestor** on the recursion stack.
3. **Deterministic Single-Successor Systems ($f : V \to V$):** Whenever every object points to *exactly one* next object (a permutation, a pointer array `next[i]`, a teleporter, or a modular iteration), the graph is a **Functional Graph** (out-degree $1$). Every connected component of a functional graph has the exact shape of a directed cycle with rooted trees feeding into the cycle.

### Decision Compass & Structural Lenses

| Sub-Pattern | Signal in the Problem Statement | DFS Mechanism & State | Key Theorem / Invariant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Connected Components & Cyclomatic Number** | "Group mutually reachable items" or "count independent cycles in an undirected network." | Track `visited[u]`; accumulate $V_c$ and $\sum \deg(u) = 2E_c$ per component. | Spanning forest uses $V_c - 1$ edges per component; $E_c - V_c + 1$ counts independent cycles. |
| **Undirected Cycle & Bipartiteness (2-Coloring)** | "Partition into 2 conflict-free sets" or "satisfy $=$ and $\neq$ binary constraints." | Maintain `color[u] \in {0, 1}`. Along edge $(u, v)$ with parity $w \in \{0,1\}$, enforce $\text{color}[v] = \text{color}[u] \oplus w$. | Undirected DFS has **no cross edges**: every non-tree edge is a back-edge to an ancestor. Odd cycle $\iff$ non-bipartite. |
| **Directed Cycle Detection (3-Color DFS)** | "Check if rules/dependencies are circular" or "find a directed cycle." | Maintain `state[u] \in {WHITE=0, GRAY=1, BLACK=2}`. `GRAY` = active on recursion stack. | Directed cycle exists $\iff$ DFS sees an edge $u \to v$ where `state[v] == GRAY`. |
| **Functional Graph ($N$ vertices, out-degree $1$)** | "Each node $i$ has a single target $p[i]$; simulate steps or find attractors." | Use 3-color DFS or Kahn's in-degree peeling to separate cycle nodes from tree nodes. | Every component is a **jellyfish** (one directed cycle + inward-pointing trees). |
| **Bridges & Cut-Edges (Tarjan's `lowlink`)** | "Which single link failure disconnects the network?" | Compute $\text{tin}[u]$ and $\text{low}[u] = \min(\text{tin}[u], \text{tin}[\text{back-edge}], \text{low}[\text{child}])$. | Tree edge $(u, v)$ is a bridge $\iff \text{low}[v] > \text{tin}[u]$. |

## Worked Problem 16.1: Quantum Phase Inverter Calibration

### Problem & Constraints

A quantum processor contains $N$ resonators ($1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$), each of which must be configured to spin state $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$. Selecting resonator $i$ for state $x_i = 1$ incurs an energy cost $c_i \ge 0$ ($0 \le c_i \le 10^9$), whereas state $x_i = 0$ is free.

You are given $M$ interference constraints ($0 \le M \le 2 \cdot 10^5$). The $j$-th constraint specifies two resonators $(u_j, v_j)$ and a required parity $w_j \in \{0, 1\}$:
- If $w_j = 0$, resonators $u_j$ and $v_j$ must be assigned **equal** states ($x_{u_j} \oplus x_{v_j} = 0$).
- If $w_j = 1$, resonators $u_j$ and $v_j$ must be assigned **opposite** states ($x_{u_j} \oplus x_{v_j} = 1$).

Determine whether a valid assignment $x \in \{0, 1\}^N$ exists, and if so, compute the **minimum total energy cost** $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i x_i$.

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong> Before reading further, ask yourself:
<ul>
  <li>Once you fix the spin $x_r \in \{0, 1\}$ of one resonator $r$ in a connected component, how many choices remain for every other resonator in that same component?</li>
  <li>How do you detect whether the constraints inside a component contradict one another?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

An assignment is a vector $x \in \{0, 1\}^N$. Checking all $2^N$ assignments takes exponential time. However, each equation $x_u \oplus x_v = w$ is a two-variable linear constraint over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Mistake 1: Greedily setting each resonator's state to $0$ (since $x_i = 0$ is free) and propagating.**\
Forcing $x_r = 0$ at an arbitrary starting node $r$ forces $x_v = 1$ for every node at odd XOR-distance from $r$. If those forced nodes have huge costs $c_v$, flipping the entire component (setting $x_r = 1$ instead) would make all those expensive nodes free!

**Mistake 2: Assuming standard bipartiteness (alternating colors on every edge) applies directly.**\
Standard bipartiteness assumes every edge requires $x_u \neq x_v$ ($w = 1$). Here, $w = 0$ edges require $x_u = x_v$. A triangle of three $w = 0$ edges has $3$ edges (an odd cycle structurally), yet it is completely satisfiable ($x_1 = x_2 = x_3$)! Conversely, a 2-edge cycle between $u$ and $v$ with one $w = 0$ edge and one $w = 1$ edge has an even number of edges, yet is unsatisfiable!

**Concrete Small Counterexample:**\
Let $N = 3$ with costs $c = [10, 100, 100]$, and constraints:
- $(1, 2, w=1)$ ($x_1 \neq x_2$),
- $(1, 3, w=1)$ ($x_1 \neq x_3$),
- $(2, 3, w=0)$ ($x_2 = x_3$).

Notice that $(1, 2, 3)$ forms a triangle, which is satisfiable because the XOR sum of edge weights around the cycle is $1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 0$. Furthermore, if we greedily set $x_1 = 0$, then $x_2 = 1$ and $x_3 = 1$, paying $100 + 100 = 200$. If we instead set $x_1 = 1$, then $x_2 = 0$ and $x_3 = 0$, paying only $c_1 = 10$.

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure

In each connected component $C$, pick an arbitrary root vertex $r$ and assign it a reference label $\text{val}[r] = 0$. As DFS traverses any edge $(u, v, w)$:
- If $v$ is unvisited, its label is uniquely forced to $\text{val}[v] = \text{val}[u] \oplus w$.
- If $v$ is already visited, the edge is a back-edge (or tree edge), and consistency requires $\text{val}[v] == \text{val}[u] \oplus w$. If this fails on any edge, the component contains a cycle of **odd XOR weight** and the entire system has no solution.

If the component is consistent, every vertex $u \in C$ is locked either to $x_r$ (if $\text{val}[u] = 0$) or to $1 - x_r$ (if $\text{val}[u] = 1$). Since components do not share edges, we choose between $x_r = 0$ and $x_r = 1$ independently for each component $C$:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Component Parity Optimization Formula:</strong>
$$\text{Cost}(C) = \min\left( \sum_{u \in C,\, \text{val}[u] = 1} c_u, \quad \sum_{u \in C,\, \text{val}[u] = 0} c_u \right)$$
$$\text{Total Minimum Cost} = \sum_{\text{components } C} \text{Cost}(C)$$
</div>

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

struct Edge {
    int to;
    int weight;
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int N, M;
    if (!(cin >> N >> M)) return 0;
    vector<long long> cost(N + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) cin >> cost[i];

    vector<vector<Edge>> adj(N + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
        int u, v, w;
        cin >> u >> v >> w;
        adj[u].push_back({v, w});
        adj[v].push_back({u, w});
    }

    vector<int> val(N + 1, -1);
    bool possible = true;
    long long total_min_cost = 0;

    for (int i = 1; i <= N && possible; ++i) {
        if (val[i] != -1) continue;

        long long sum_val[2] = {0, 0};
        vector<int> stk = {i};
        val[i] = 0;

        while (!stk.empty()) {
            int u = stk.back();
            stk.pop_back();
            sum_val[val[u]] += cost[u];

            for (const auto& e : adj[u]) {
                int expected = val[u] ^ e.weight;
                if (val[e.to] == -1) {
                    val[e.to] = expected;
                    stk.push_back(e.to);
                } else if (val[e.to] != expected) {
                    possible = false;
                }
            }
        }
        total_min_cost += min(sum_val[0], sum_val[1]);
    }

    if (!possible) cout << -1 << "\n";
    else cout << total_min_cost << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Proof of Completeness via Spanning Tree Fundamental Cycles:**
In each connected component $C$, the DFS tree $T_C$ fixes a unique candidate assignment $\text{val}[u] = \text{val}[r] \oplus \text{dist}_{\oplus}(r, u)$ along tree paths. Every non-tree edge $e = (u, v, w)$ defines a fundamental cycle $C_e$. If $\text{val}[u] \oplus \text{val}[v] = w$ holds for every non-tree edge, then our explicit construction satisfies all $M$ edges simultaneously (both for $\text{val}[r] = 0$ and $\text{val}[r] = 1$). Conversely, if $\text{val}[u] \oplus \text{val}[v] \neq w$ for some edge $e$, summing the equations $x_a \oplus x_b = w_{ab}$ around the fundamental cycle $C_e$ yields $0 = 1$ (since every vertex appears twice on the left-hand side and cancels out, while the right-hand side sums to $1$), providing an airtight certificate of impossibility.

## Worked Problem 16.2: Autonomous Drone Relay Loops

### Problem & Constraints

In a sector of $N$ relay beacons ($1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$), each beacon $u$ is programmed with a single primary forwarding target $f[u] \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ (note that $f[u] = u$ is possible). A diagnostic packet launched at beacon $u$ hops deterministically $u \to f[u] \to f[f[u]] \to \dots$ until it visits some beacon for the **second** time, at which moment the packet halts to prevent infinite looping.

For every starting beacon $u \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, compute $L[u]$: the total number of **distinct** beacons visited by a packet launched from $u$ before it halts.

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong> Before reading further, ask yourself:
<ul>
  <li>If a graph has $N$ vertices and every vertex has out-degree $1$, what does each connected component look like?</li>
  <li>If beacon $u$ is outside the cycle and steps to $v = f[u]$, how does $L[u]$ relate to $L[v]$? What if $u$ is already *on* a cycle?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

Simulating the walk $u \to f[u] \to \dots$ from each starting vertex $u$ independently until a duplicate vertex is seen takes $O(N)$ steps per vertex in the worst case (e.g., a long path feeding into a small cycle, or a single $N$-cycle). Across all $N$ starting vertices, direct simulation costs $\Theta(N^2)$ time, which times out for $N = 2 \cdot 10^5$.

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Mistake 1: Treating `visited` globally as a boolean and setting $L[u] = 1 + L[f[u]]$ whenever $f[u]$ was ever visited.**\
If $u$ is **on a cycle** of length $C$, both $u$ and $f[u]$ visit the exact same $C$ vertices: $L[u] = L[f[u]] = C$, **not** $1 + L[f[u]]$!

**Mistake 2: Confusing a cross-edge to an already-solved branch (`BLACK`) with a back-edge closing a new cycle (`GRAY`).**

**Concrete Small Counterexample:**\
Let $N = 4$ with $f = [2, 3, 2, 2]$ ($1 \to 2 \leftrightarrow 3$, and $4 \to 2$).
- Cycle is $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ of length $2$, so $L[2] = L[3] = 2$.
- Vertex $1$ steps to $2$, visiting $\{1, 2, 3\}$, so $L[1] = 1 + L[2] = 3$.
- When we later start a traversal from vertex $4$, its edge $4 \to 2$ hits vertex $2$, which is already visited! If we falsely think "hitting a visited vertex means $4 \to 2$ closes a cycle," we would misclassify $4$ as part of a cycle. This is why we must distinguish `GRAY` (active on the current walk) from `BLACK` (already fully resolved).

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure

Because every vertex has out-degree $1$, following pointers from any `WHITE` vertex $u$ produces a single deterministic chain of `GRAY` vertices. Eventually, the chain must hit a non-`WHITE` vertex $w$:

1. **Case A (`state[w] == GRAY`):** Vertex $w$ is on our current active chain! Since every vertex has out-degree $1$, all vertices on our active stack from $w$ up to the current tip form a **directed cycle** $C$. If that cycle has $k$ vertices, then for every $c \in C$, we immediately know $L[c] = k$. All earlier vertices on our chain before $w$ are tree ancestors feeding into $w$.
2. **Case B (`state[w] == BLACK`):** Vertex $w$ belongs to an earlier pass and its answer $L[w]$ is already finalized. None of the vertices on our current active chain are on a cycle; they all feed into $w$.

In both cases, once the cycle portion (if any) is assigned $L[c] = |C|$, every remaining tree vertex $u$ on the active chain satisfies:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Functional Graph Decomposition Equations:</strong>
$$L[u] = \begin{cases} |C| & \text{if } u \text{ lies on the directed cycle } C, \\ 1 + L[f[u]] & \text{if } u \text{ is a tree vertex feeding toward the cycle.} \end{cases}$$
</div>

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int N;
    if (!(cin >> N)) return 0;
    vector<int> f(N + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) cin >> f[i];

    // state: 0 = WHITE, 1 = GRAY (on current chain), 2 = BLACK (solved)
    vector<int> state(N + 1, 0);
    vector<int> L(N + 1, 0);

    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        if (state[i] != 0) continue;

        vector<int> chain;
        int cur = i;
        while (state[cur] == 0) {
            state[cur] = 1;
            chain.push_back(cur);
            cur = f[cur];
        }

        if (state[cur] == 1) {
            // cur is GRAY: locate cur in chain to extract the directed cycle
            auto it = find(chain.begin(), chain.end(), cur);
            int cycle_len = static_cast<int>(chain.end() - it);
            while (chain.back() != cur) {
                int u = chain.back();
                chain.pop_back();
                L[u] = cycle_len;
                state[u] = 2;
            }
            // Also finalize cur itself
            chain.pop_back();
            L[cur] = cycle_len;
            state[cur] = 2;
        }

        // Remaining nodes in chain are tree ancestors feeding into solved nodes
        while (!chain.empty()) {
            int u = chain.back();
            chain.pop_back();
            L[u] = 1 + L[f[u]];
            state[u] = 2;
        }
    }

    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        cout << L[i] << (i == N ? "" : " ");
    }
    cout << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Complexity & Correctness Proof:**
Every vertex $u \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ transitions $0 \to 1 \to 2$ (`WHITE` $\to$ `GRAY` $\to$ `BLACK`) at most once. Therefore, each vertex is pushed onto and popped from `chain` at most once across the entire run, guaranteeing $O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ auxiliary space—with no recursion stack overflow even if the graph is a single chain of length $2 \cdot 10^5$.

**Small-Case Oracle:** For $N \le 7$, enumerate all $N^N$ functional graphs (or random samples), compute $L[u]$ by brute-force `std::set` simulation from each vertex, and assert equality with the linear 3-color chain solver. Include self-loops ($f[u] = u$, cycle of size $1$) and lollipop graphs.

***

# Section 17 — Topological Sorting and DAG DP

## The Discovery & Modeling Approach

A **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** is the universal backbone of dynamic programming. Every DP recurrence you have ever written—over array prefixes, grid coordinates, tree subtrees, or bitmasks—is secretly an evaluation of vertices along a topological order of a DAG. When a problem gives you an arbitrary dependency structure rather than a regular grid or array, you must **construct the topological order explicitly** before evaluating the recurrence.

### Recognizing Hidden Topological Sort and DAG DP Problems

1. **Precedence / Prerequisite Constraints:** Statements containing rules of the form *"$A$ must occur before $B$"*, *"module $u$ compiles before module $v$"*, *"inequality $x_u < x_v$"*, or *"recover an unknown alphabet order from a sorted dictionary"* translate directly into directed edges $u \to v$. A valid linear arrangement exists if and only if the directed graph is acyclic.
2. **Longest Path or Path Counting in a Directed Graph:** In a general graph, Longest Simple Path and `#P`-complete path counting are intractable because paths can loop. The moment the graph is guaranteed to be a DAG (or after you verify acyclicity via Kahn's algorithm or 3-color DFS), longest paths, shortest paths with negative weights, and total path counts all become linear-time $O(V + E)$ dynamic programs!
3. **Lexicographically Extremal Permutations under Precedence:** When multiple topological orderings exist and the problem asks for a specific tie-breaking rule, **stop and check the objective carefully**:
   - *"Make the sequence lexicographically smallest"* (minimize the 1st element, then 2nd, etc.) $\implies$ Min-heap Kahn's algorithm on the **forward** graph.
   - *"Make label $1$ appear as early as possible, then label $2$ as early as possible, ..."* (minimize the inverse permutation $\text{pos}[1]$, then $\text{pos}[2]$, etc.) $\implies$ Max-heap Kahn's algorithm on the **reversed** graph, filling positions from $N$ down to $1$!

### Decision Compass & Structural Lenses

| Sub-Pattern | Signal in the Problem Statement | Algorithmic Mechanism | Complexity & Key Invariant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Kahn's In-Degree Peeling** | "Find any valid execution order or report a cyclic deadlock." | Maintain `indeg[v]`; push all `indeg[v] == 0` into queue; pop $u$, decrement `indeg[v]` for $u \to v$. | $O(V + E)$. Graph is a DAG $\iff$ exactly $V$ vertices are popped. Unpopped vertices contain a cycle. |
| **Push / Pull DAG DP** | "Longest path, critical-path scheduling, or number of ways from $s$ to $t$ in a DAG." | Compute topological order $T[1..V]$; relax $dp[v] = \bigoplus_{u \to v} f(dp[u], w(u, v))$ in order of $T$. | $O(V + E)$. When $u$ is processed, all its predecessors have already finalized their $dp$ values. |
| **Lexicographically Smallest Topological Order** | "Among all valid schedules, minimize the ID at index $1$, then index $2$, etc." | Replace Kahn's FIFO queue with a **min-priority queue** (`greater<int>`) on the forward graph. | $O((V + E) \log V)$. Greedily places the smallest available zero-indegree vertex at the front. |
| **Reverse-Graph Priority Kahn** | "Prioritize placing vertex $1$ as early as possible, then vertex $2$, etc." | Reverse all edges; run a **max-priority queue** from the back (position $N$ down to $1$). | $O((V + E) \log V)$. Deferring large labels as late as possible pulls small labels as early as possible. |
| **Implicit Monotone Attribute DAG** | "Move only to strictly higher altitude / energy / value." | Direct edges $u \to v$ whenever $h[u] < h[v]$; sort vertices by $h$ or run Kahn's algorithm. | Any strict inequality $h[u] < h[v]$ on edges guarantees acyclicity automatically! |

  <text x="460" y="36" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Section 17 Structural Lens: Topological Linearization &amp; Forward vs. Reverse Priority</text>

  <!-- Left: DAG Linearization + DP -->

## Worked Problem 17.1: Compiler Pipeline Critical Path & Bottleneck Count

### Problem & Constraints

A distributed build system compiles $N$ software targets ($1 \le N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) connected by $M$ directed dependency edges ($0 \le M \le 3 \cdot 10^5$). An edge $u \to v$ means target $u$ must finish compiling before target $v$ can begin, plus a data-transfer latency of $w(u, v) \ge 0$ milliseconds ($0 \le w \le 10^9$). Compiling target $u$ itself takes $t[u] > 0$ milliseconds ($1 \le t[u] \le 10^9$). Any number of targets whose dependencies are satisfied may compile in parallel.

1. First, verify whether the dependency graph is acyclic. If a cycle exists, output `CYCLE`.
2. Otherwise, compute the **minimum total time $T_{\text{min}}$** required to finish all $N$ targets, and for each target $u$, determine the number of **critical dependency chains** starting at $u$ that achieve the global completion time $T_{\text{min}}$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

<div class="pause-box">
<strong>Pause &amp; Discover:</strong> Before reading further, ask yourself:
<ul>
  <li>Why can we compute the longest path in $O(N + M)$ time here when Longest Path is NP-hard in general graphs?</li>
  <li>How do we combine earliest-finish DP (forward along topological order) with latest-start DP or suffix path counting (backward along topological order)?</li>
</ul>
</div>

### Step 1 — Exact Model & Bottleneck

With unlimited parallelism, every target $v$ starts at the exact moment all of its prerequisites $u$ have finished compiling and transferring their outputs to $v$. Thus the earliest completion time $E[v]$ of target $v$ is the maximum weight of any directed path ending at $v$ ( summing both vertex durations $t[\cdot]$ and edge latencies $w(\cdot, \cdot)$).

Enumerating all paths from sources to sinks is exponential (for instance, a chain of $N/2$ diamonds has $2^{N/2}$ paths).

### Step 2 — Tempting Mistakes & Counterexample

**Mistake 1: Running Dijkstra (with negated weights or max-heap) to find the longest path.**\
Dijkstra's greedy invariant fails completely for longest paths (or negative-weight shortest paths): when a vertex $v$ is popped from a heap, a later multi-hop path $u \to x \to v$ can arrive with a *strictly larger* completion time, forcing $v$ and all of $v$'s descendants to be re-expanded exponentially many times on a diamond DAG!

**Mistake 2: Counting critical paths by incrementing `ways[v] += ways[u]` whenever $u \to v$ improves $E[v]$, without resetting `ways[v]` when $E[v]$ strictly increases, or forgetting that the question asks for critical chains *starting at $u$ and reaching the global maximum $T_{\text{min}}$*.**

**Concrete Small Counterexample:**\
Suppose $N = 3$ with vertex times $t = [10, 10, 10]$ and edges $1 \to 2$ ($w=5$), $1 \to 3$ ($w=20$), $2 \to 3$ ($w=5$).
- Path $1 \to 3$ finishes at $10 + 20 + 10 = 40$.
- Path $1 \to 2 \to 3$ finishes at $10 + 5 + 10 + 5 + 10 = 40$.
If we used a heap-based relaxation before all predecessors of $3$ were finalized, $3$ would first be relaxed via $1 \to 3$ to $40$ and popped before $2$ is even expanded via $2 \to 3$.

### Step 3 — The Turn: Discovering the Structure

Kahn's algorithm produces a topological order $\text{topo}[0..N-1]$ in $O(N + M)$ time and simultaneously certifies acyclicity: the graph is a DAG if and only if $|\text{topo}| = N$.

Once $\text{topo}$ is fixed, we run two linear scans over $\text{topo}$:
1. **Forward Scan (Earliest Finish $E[v]$):** Initialize $E[v] = t[v]$. Iterate $u$ left-to-right in $\text{topo}$; for each edge $u \to v$ with weight $w$:
   $$E[v] = \max\bigl(E[v],\; E[u] + w + t[v]\bigr)$$
   Then $T_{\text{min}} = \max_{1 \le v \le N} E[v]$.
2. **Backward Scan (Longest Remaining Tail $R[u]$ & Critical Chain Count $W[u]$):** To know which chains starting at $u$ achieve $T_{\text{min}}$, let $R[u]$ be the maximum time of a path starting at $u$ (including $t[u]$), and $W[u]$ be the number of paths starting at $u$ of total weight $R[u]$. Iterate $u$ **right-to-left** in $\text{topo}$:

<div class="formula-card">
<strong>Forward-Backward Critical DAG Recurrences:</strong>
$$R[u] = t[u] + \max\bigl(\{0\} \cup \{ w(u, v) + R[v] \mid u \to v \in E \}\bigr)$$
$$W[u] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } R[u] = t[u] \text{ (no outgoing edge extends } u\text{)}, \\ \displaystyle\sum_{\substack{u \to v \in E \\ t[u] + w(u,v) + R[v] = R[u]}} W[v] \pmod{10^9+7} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
$$\text{Critical chains starting at } u \text{ that achieve } T_{\text{min}} = \begin{cases} W[u] & \text{if } R[u] = T_{\text{min}}, \\ 0 & \text{if } R[u] < T_{\text{min}}. \end{cases}$$
</div>

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <algorithm>

using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

struct Edge {
    int to;
    long long weight;
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int N, M;
    if (!(cin >> N >> M)) return 0;

    vector<long long> t(N + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) cin >> t[i];

    vector<vector<Edge>> adj(N + 1);
    vector<int> indeg(N + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        long long w;
        cin >> u >> v >> w;
        adj[u].push_back({v, w});
        indeg[v]++;
    }

    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    }

    vector<int> topo;
    topo.reserve(N);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        topo.push_back(u);
        for (const auto& e : adj[u]) {
            if (--indeg[e.to] == 0) {
                q.push(e.to);
            }
        }
    }

    if (static_cast<int>(topo.size()) < N) {
        cout << "CYCLE\n";
        return 0;
    }

    // Forward DP: earliest finish time E[u]
    vector<long long> E(N + 1);
    long long T_min = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) E[i] = t[i];
    for (int u : topo) {
        T_min = max(T_min, E[u]);
        for (const auto& e : adj[u]) {
            E[e.to] = max(E[e.to], E[u] + e.weight + t[e.to]);
        }
    }

    // Backward DP: longest tail R[u] and count W[u]
    vector<long long> R(N + 1, 0);
    vector<long long> W(N + 1, 1);
    for (int i = N - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
        int u = topo[i];
        R[u] = t[u];
        W[u] = 1; // Base case: chain of just {u}
        for (const auto& e : adj[u]) {
            long long cand = t[u] + e.weight + R[e.to];
            if (cand > R[u]) {
                R[u] = cand;
                W[u] = W[e.to];
            } else if (cand == R[u]) {
                W[u] = (W[u] + W[e.to]) % MOD;
            }
        }
    }

    cout << T_min << "\n";
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        long long ans = (R[i] == T_min) ? W[i] : 0;
        cout << ans << (i == N ? "" : " ");
    }
    cout << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

### Step 5 — Two-Way Proof & Small-Case Oracle

**Proof of Cycle Certificate and Path Bijection:**
- *Cycle Certificate:* Any vertex in a directed cycle has at least one predecessor inside the cycle, so its `indeg` can never drop to $0$. Conversely, if the remaining subgraph is nonempty and has no zero-indegree vertex, walking backward along incoming edges from any remaining vertex visits a repeated vertex within $\le N$ steps, exhibiting a cycle.
- *DP Induction:* Because `topo` places every $u$ before $v$ whenever $u \to v$, in the reverse loop every $v$ has already finalized $(R[v], W[v])$ before $u$ inspects edge $u \to v$. Since $t[v] > 0$ and $w(u, v) \ge 0$, every outgoing edge strictly increases $cand \ge t[u] + t[v] > t[u]$, so the base case $W[u] = 1$ (stopping at $u$) is cleanly overwritten as soon as at least one outgoing edge exists.
